title: The morning preview
hookLine: Marcus tells himself at dawn he'll meet the meddling and the ungrateful, and that they are his kin (Meditations 2.1)

cards: Marcus Aurelius was emperor of Rome, a man with every reason to expect the best from people: nearly everyone he met had to be polite to him.

And yet the notebook he kept, written to himself, now called the Meditations, opens its second book with a warning to himself, like someone packing an umbrella on a cloudy day. Today there will be difficult people.
Plan for it. It starts a new pair of practices, one for the start of the day and one for the end. This one is the morning preview.

teach.b: George Long's 1862 translation opens the passage like this: Begin the morning by saying to thyself, I shall meet with the busy-body, the ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsocial.
It sounds grim, a list of every annoying person you'll see before lunch. But Marcus doesn't stop there.

teach.h: THEY DON'T KNOW GOOD FROM BAD.
teach.b: He says why they act this way: they don't know what is truly good and bad. Then comes the turn.
The person who wrongs him, he says, is his kin, not only by blood, but because they share the same intelligence and the same portion of the divine.
We were made to work together, he writes, like two hands, two feet, two eyelids, the upper and lower rows of teeth. To work against each other is against nature.
So he can't be harmed by them, and he won't be angry with them. The preview isn't pessimism. It's the opposite of being ambushed.
Expect a smooth day, and the first rude person lands like a slap. Say first, some people today will be hard, and they're my people anyway, and the same rudeness lands like weather.

You saw it coming, and you'd already decided how to meet it. The preview takes one minute, and it moves your best self from the evening, when you think of the perfect reply, to the morning, when it can still be used.

how: Some people who draw on the Stoics begin the day with a short preview, often reading or recalling Meditations 2.1 and picturing the hard moments ahead and how they want to meet them.

o: a Greek teacher who wrote dialogues on justice
the emperor who previewed his hard day each dawn
a Roman general who wrote about winning battles

games.q: what's inside Marcus's morning — tap the pairs.
p: they don't know good from bad

s: Marcus wrote the Meditations as a book for the public
it reads as a notebook written to himself, maybe never meant for other readers.
Marcus calls the person who wrongs him his kin
they share the same intelligence and a portion of the divine.
the morning preview is a way of expecting the worst
it's the opposite of being ambushed: you decide ahead of time how to meet the hard parts.

games.q: you're Marcus. you've just told yourself you'll meet the ungrateful and the arrogant today. what do you add next?
o: so I'll avoid them all day.
they are my kin, and I won't be angry with them.
so I'll be ready to put them in their place.
games.why: he says they are his kin, made to work with him like two hands. he can't be harmed by them, and won't be angry with them.

practice: Walk through today in your mind, from now until bed, and find where it might get hard: a slow colleague, a tired partner, a stranger in traffic.
Picture meeting that moment the way you'd like to, steady, fair, kind, and remind yourself: they're people, like me, doing what they think is right. Then let the picture go, and breathe.

wordCard.voice: Marcus. A minute at the start of the day to expect the hard parts, and decide how to meet them, the way he did at dawn. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: at dawn, from early morning. Marcus wrote in Greek, and this is the first word of Meditations 2.1.

carryVoice: Your line: I'll meet them kindly. When the busy-body shows up right on schedule, you saw them coming. That's day one hundred four.
